card.hook: Here's a street where the roof does half the work for you. It frames the shot, pulls the eye down the walkway, and fills it with colour, signs and people.
card.stand_here: Stand on the covered pedestrian part of Jalan Hang Kasturi, beside Central Market. It's about 300 m north of the market, so walk about 300 m north to reach the walkway. Face along the street so the kiosks and stalls sit on either side of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the walkway. Switch to 0.5x to fit in the whole length of the street and the roof, then go to 2x for signs and stall displays.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walkway up with the middle of the frame, then keep your phone level so the roofline stays straight.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day for fewer people in the walkway. The roof gives some cover from sun and rain, so this spot works in most weather.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the drop-pin sculpture next to the main entrance, with the historic frontage behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. The covered street beside the market is a good backup.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the pavement in front of the light blue facade so the whole building fits, while you pose by the drop-pin sculpture.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the public areas, but respect private stalls and any 'no photography' signs. Ask before taking close-ups of vendors or their goods, especially when they're busy. Check the front of the building for works or barriers before you plan a facade shot.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get the whole walkway in one frame, roofline straight, with a splash of colour from the stalls.
card.good_to_know: Central Market began in 1888 as a wet market, and the Art Deco building you see today was finished in 1937. It was saved from demolition, renovated in 1985-86 and relaunched as Pasar Budaya (the Cultural Market). The walkway links to Kasturi Walk, which opened in 2011 and is known for snack and souvenir stalls and street musicians.

card.hook: Two 88-storey towers, one lake, and a good shot at a mirror image if the water behaves. Bring a little patience and you'll walk away with a postcard.
card.stand_here: Head into KLCC Park, walk to the lake edge on the lake side, and face the towers across the water. You'll get both towers, the greenery and the fountain area in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x with the phone upright so both towers fit, with some water and greenery below. Standing right at the water and want more park around the towers? Try zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) picks out the top floors and the sky bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand straight, and keep the phone level instead of tilting it up.
card.best_time: Go for blue hour, from about 30 to 60 minutes before sunset until full darkness, when the sky is deep blue and the towers are lit. Arrive before sunset, because the walkways get busy and the best spots at the water's edge fill up.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza KLCC, the open plaza right at the base of the towers, or the street corner in front of NZ Curry House at Jalan Yap Kwan Seng and Jalan Ampang. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the towers rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the footbridge over Symphony Lake in KLCC Park and shoot you with both towers in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The Jalan Yap Kwan Seng and Jalan Ampang junction is busy, so keep an eye on your surroundings while you pose. Check the official site before you go for closures, photography rules and any visits inside the towers.
card.challenge: Get both towers standing perfectly straight on the gridlines, with the water filling the bottom of the frame. Bonus points if the reflection is calm enough to fool your friends.
card.good_to_know: The towers are 451.9 m tall and were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004. They're still the tallest twin towers. They opened on 31 August 1999 on the site of the old Selangor Turf Club race track, and the steel and glass skin echoes patterns from Islamic art.

card.hook: A giant green Hanuman, a cave mouth full of painted figures, and a monkey eyeing your snacks. All three are at the foot of the hill, away from the staircase crowd.
card.stand_here: Stand at Ramayana Cave, just outside the entrance beside the Hanuman statue at the foot of the hill, to the left of the main staircase. Face the statue and let the painted figures fill the lower corners of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the statue and the painted figures. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze the statue and the cave entrance into one frame. Try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for faces and paintwork. It also keeps you a polite distance from the monkeys.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright paint and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Softer light earlier or later in the day is kinder to bright paint than harsh midday sun. Skip Thaipusam if you want a quiet frame, because the forecourt gets very crowded.
card.selfie_here: Use your front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a little low and out in front of you. That way the statue and the colourful figures fit in behind your shoulder. Tilt the phone slightly until the statue stands up straight.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash and no drones. Photography inside the caves is restricted, and you should ask permission before photographing worshippers. Monkeys are common, so keep your phone and food close. This is a working place of worship, so check the official site for ticketing and opening hours before you go.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful painted face around the cave entrance and fill your screen with it. Bonus points if no monkey photobombs you.
card.good_to_know: Batu Caves is a limestone hill about 13 km north of central Kuala Lumpur, around 325 m tall. The Hanuman statue is 15 m high, and the Hanuman temple opened in November 2001. The famous golden Murugan statue is 42.7 m, and the rainbow staircase has 272 steps, built in 1940 and repainted in 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Ramayana Cave, just outside the entrance beside the Hanuman statue at the foot of the hill, to the left of the main staircase. Face the statue and let the painted figures fill the lower corners of your shot.

card.hook: This park covers 91.6 hectares, and your phone only needs one tidy corner of it. Pick the Sunken Garden, a round lawn set down in a bowl like a secret garden.
card.stand_here: Stand at the hedge arch at the Sunken Garden's entrance and look down into the bowl. The arch frames the circular lawn, and the star fountain gives your eye somewhere to land.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which suits the view framed by the arch. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze in the whole bowl, or 2x to pick out the fountain and the white flower pots.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the arch's edges straight along them, and put the fountain in the centre or on a crossing of the lines.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. One guide says the light is best here then.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, stand under the golden honeycomb canopy at Laman Perdana. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt up a little so the canopy fills the space behind your shoulder. You can also try the Sunken Garden hedge-arch entrance, with the round garden and star fountain behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to crouch low on the main garden square while you stand in front of the Laman Perdana canopy, so the canopy fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Opening times and fees can vary, and a weekend fee may apply to the Orchid and Hibiscus gardens. Commercial photography and drones may need a permit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the eight points of the star fountain in your photo, then see if you can get the arch edges perfectly straight too.
card.good_to_know: This was Kuala Lumpur's first large recreational park. It was started in 1888 by Alfred Venning, the British State Treasurer of Selangor, who had a stream dammed to make the ornamental lake. The gardens were formally opened on 13 May 1889.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the hedge arch at the Sunken Garden's entrance and look down into the bowl. The arch frames the circular lawn, and the star fountain gives your eye somewhere to land.

card.hook: Picture a 678.9-metre tower of glass diamonds poking up over painted walls and old shophouse roofs. That's the Chinatown shot of Merdeka 118, and it's the one everyone wants.
card.stand_here: Stand on Old Kuala Lumpur Street Art, the alleyway in Chinatown (search that name on Google Maps). Face north-east and the tower rises above the painted walls and Chinatown buildings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the street art and buildings stay in the picture with the tower above them. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Save 0.5x for the forecourt at the tower's base.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the phone upright, switch on gridlines, put the street art in the bottom of the frame and let the tower fill the top, then tap the tower and slide it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the glass.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the alley is quieter. Sunrise or golden hour is lovely from Taman Rekreasi Pudu Ulu, and after dark the tower is lit, so try night mode.
card.selfie_here: Head to the rooftop lookout at Look At 118 (Jalan Hang Jebat side), stand at the railing with the tower rising behind you, and use the front camera. Or try the Petaling Street mural by Big Boss HSP next to Five Snowmen: stand at an angle and shoot low so the painted shapes line up with the tower's tip.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the grounds of Al-Sultan Abdullah Mosque, near the fountains and water features, and pose so the tower fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in public areas, but some zones may have limits, so check signs or ask staff. The area around the stadiums has little shade, so bring water and a hat in the middle of the day.
card.challenge: Take one upright shot where the painted wall is at the bottom and the tower's tip just reaches the top of the frame, then see if your friends can spot the diamond pattern.
card.good_to_know: Merdeka 118, now officially Merdeka Maybank Tower, is the tallest building in Malaysia and the second tallest in the world, with 118 storeys. Its glass diamond panels are meant to reflect Malaysia's variety of people, and the shape is said to echo Tunku Abdul Rahman's raised hand as he called out "Merdeka!" in 1957. The tower was completed in November 2023, but the wider complex was still mostly closed, so plan on photographing it from outside.

card.hook: Picture a zebra crossing at night, with a wave of people stepping out, traffic streaking past and a seven-storey mall glowing behind them. That's Bukit Bintang, and you don't need to be a photographer to get a great shot of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement at the kerb beside the Jalan Bukit Bintang crossing, near the Pavilion Kuala Lumpur entrance. Face across the crossing towards the lit mall frontage.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the crossing and the mall. If the pavement is too crowded to step back, tap 0.5x. Use 2x or more to pick out a single walker or a neon sign without moving.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest sign, then slide the brightness down a little so the neon doesn't burn out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the neon and mall lights are on and the traffic trails show up. Weekends are the busiest and give you the liveliest crowds.
card.selfie_here: Head to the far-side corner of the crossing, by the traffic light that overlooks the McDonald's. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the junction and its painted zebra lines behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to go inside Bukit Bintang monorail station, where they can shoot down onto the crossing of Jalan Bukit Bintang and Jalan Sultan Ismail while you pose at the crossing.
card.rules_and_safety: Shoot from the pavement, never stand in the road, and cross only when the signal allows. It gets packed at weekends, so keep out of people's way. If you want to take photos inside Pavilion or another mall, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a group to step into the gap in front of the lit mall, then catch the moment they become the star of your photo.
card.good_to_know: Bukit Bintang is Kuala Lumpur's main shopping and entertainment district. Jalan Bukit Bintang is about 3.4 km long, and the district is named after a hill of roughly 50 m that once stood nearby. Pavilion was built in late 2007 and is a seven-storey mall. If you have time for a second scene, Jalan Alor is a lively night food street.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement at the kerb beside the Jalan Bukit Bintang crossing, near the Pavilion Kuala Lumpur entrance. Face across the crossing towards the lit mall frontage.

card.hook: Picture a cricket field with a country's birthday party hidden in its past. At midnight on 30 to 31 August 1957, the British flag came down here and the Malayan flag went up for the first time.
card.stand_here: At Independence Square, stand about 100 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south across the field toward the flagpole. The old Sultan Abdul Samad Building runs along one side of your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the lawn, the flagpole and the building in one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the top of the flagpole or the building's details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the flagpole on one of the vertical lines, so it doesn't split your photo down the middle.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon. The light is softer and the square is usually quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement in front of the Sultan Abdul Samad Building, which visitors often pick as the most popular photo stop on the square. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand out on the lawn on the opposite side of the square, facing the building, while you stand in front of it so the whole building is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: There's a big, busy road right in front of the Sultan Abdul Samad Building, so take care when posing or stepping back. The building has been reported as under renovation, with scaffolding over parts of it. Access to the square has also been reported as restricted at times, so check before you set out.
card.challenge: Hunt down the round black marble plaque where the new flag first went up, and see if you can get it in your photo with the flagpole rising behind it.
card.good_to_know: Independence Square is Dataran Merdeka in Malay. It used to be the Padang, the cricket field of the Selangor Club. The flagpole at the southern end is 95 metres tall, one of the tallest in the world. The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, in Indo-Saracenic style, has housed government offices since 1897.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: At Independence Square, stand about 100 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south across the field toward the flagpole. The old Sultan Abdul Samad Building runs along one side of your view.

card.hook: Picture a ceiling made of red lanterns, with a stack of ornate roofs peeking out behind them. That's the Thean Hou Temple courtyard, and it's hard to take a bad photo here.
card.stand_here: Head into the lantern courtyards, where the phone icon on the map sits. Plant your feet in a clear spot under the lanterns and point your phone up, so the rows of lanterns fill the frame with the roofline behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the lanterns and roofline both fit. Use 1x for general views of the courtyards and buildings. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carvings, roof ornaments and the zodiac statues.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up one row of lanterns with a vertical line, and keep the roofline in the top third.
card.best_time: Early morning around opening time usually means softer light and fewer people. In the evening the lit lanterns glow, so switch on night mode and hold your phone against a pillar or your chest while it captures. Festivals like Chinese New Year are when the lantern displays look their best, but expect more people.
card.selfie_here: Try the dragon sculpture at the end of the stairs, on the way down from the main hall, where the temple is in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a little low so the temple fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to shoot straight-on from the main staircase, so the six tiers and red-and-gold roofs fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine, but be considerate of worshippers when you take selfies. Keep flash off in the prayer halls, and ask permission before photographing worshippers or monks.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the best photo of KL Tower isn't taken at KL Tower. Its base sits on a hill and is awkward to shoot from, so we're sending you to a lake instead.
card.stand_here: Stand at the water's edge in Taman Tasik Titiwangsa, the lakeside park north of the tower, by the park's big central lake. Walk along the shore, face south, and look for the slim shaft and pod on the skyline.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the faraway tower closer. Use zoom 1x if you want more lake and skyline. Skip 0.5x for the tower itself, because it shrinks to a tiny sliver.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines instead of the middle, and keep a good strip of water in the bottom half so the reflection fills the foreground.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are the times recommended for the lake. It's also usually quieter here than at the tower's own entrance area.
card.selfie_here: Head to the treetop canopy walk in the Bukit Nanas Forest Reserve, right beside the tower, which is described as a photogenic spot. card.ask_someone: At the big central lake, ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand by the water and they face you, so the lake and the distant tower sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Taman Tasik Titiwangsa is a public park, but check the official site before you go for any local rules or closures.
card.challenge: Find the calmest patch of water you can, then get the tower and its wobbly twin reflection in one shot without a single ripple ruining it.
card.good_to_know: KL Tower is 421 metres tall and opened to the public on 23 July 1996, when it was the tallest structure in Malaysia. The Petronas Twin Towers overtook it three years later. It's still the highest viewpoint in the city that the public can visit, with a revolving restaurant up in the pod.

card.hook: Just around the corner from the haggling and market noise, there's a narrow alley of restored shophouses with murals on the walls and red lanterns strung overhead. It's the tidy, calm picture Petaling Street doesn't usually show you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the entrance of Kwai Chai Hong, on the Petaling Street side, in the lantern alley. Face down the narrow lane so the shophouses, murals and lanterns run away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x in the narrow alley so the lanterns, murals and shophouse walls all fit. Then try 1x for a more natural look. Out on Jalan Petaling, zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) can pick out one lantern, a stall or a face from further back.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the alley's centre up with the middle grid line, so the lanterns lead the eye straight down the lane.
card.best_time: Go before 10 am or after 5 pm. In the evening the lanterns are lit against the sky. Weekends and holidays are very crowded, and the lanterns may not be up all year.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie under the traditional archway at the entrance to Petaling Street, near Wisma Fui Chiu. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone offers it) and let the arch, red lanterns and busy stalls fill the background over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Petaling Street is an open pedestrian street and Kwai Chai Hong is described as free to visit. Check the official site before you go for any current restrictions or closures.
card.challenge: Find one of the murals with a QR code and get it in your shot with a red lantern hanging above it.
card.good_to_know: In Cantonese, Petaling Street is called Chee Cheong Kai, meaning Starch Factory Street. It's named after a tapioca mill opened here by the Chinese Kapitan Yap Ah Loy. The green roof and the arches at each end date from a makeover in 2003, and the lantern alley has six murals with QR codes that tell of residents' lives in earlier times.

card.hook: Flamingos and pelicans wading about in the shallows, with thick green leaves behind them like a painted backdrop. That's the first thing you see at Kuala Lumpur Bird Park, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Head to Flamingo Pond, just inside the main entrance, and stand at the pond's edge. Face across the water so the wading birds are in front of you and the greenery is behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the birds and the greenery both fit. Go to 2x-5x for a single bird (higher zooms depend on your phone), and use 0.5x in the walk-through aviary or by the waterfall to fit the whole scene.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the birds on one of the lines, then tap a bird and slide brighter/darker down a touch if the water looks glary.
card.best_time: There's no single best time, and the shade means it works all day. Earlier is probably quieter, and the birds may be livelier.
card.selfie_here: Take it at Flamingo Pond on the pond edge, with the flamingos and leafy greenery behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little high so the birds stay over your shoulder. The Zone 4 parrot area also works during the daily feeding, which runs 10am to 5pm.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch your step around the lakes and waterfall, because it can be slippery. Drones are reportedly not allowed, and professional or commercial photography may need a permit. Check the signs near feeding areas and bird shows.
card.challenge: Get a flamingo and a pelican in the same frame without a single bit of netting at the top.
card.good_to_know: It's about 8.5 hectares, and it's one of the world's largest covered bird parks. More than 3,000 birds from over 200 species live under the netting, and roughly nine in ten are local. It was first planned in 1987 and sits next to the Perdana Botanical Gardens.

card.hook: Right at the edge of Chinatown, a tower of painted gods rises over the traffic in five bright tiers. It's hard to walk past without getting your phone out.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Tun H.S. Lee, on the opposite sidewalk from the temple entrance, set back about 10 m. Face the temple gate so the whole gopuram fills your frame, with the street in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the road so the whole tower fits. If traffic or people stop you backing up, switch to zoom 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Hold your phone upright with the gridlines on, tap the brightest part of the tower, then slide to make it a touch darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Try the first 30 minutes after the temple opens. Worshippers with garlands are walking through the gate, and the morning light falls on the painted figures.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold the phone a little low, so the tower fits behind your shoulder. One visitor said the afternoon is quieter for self-portraits.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to shoot from the opposite sidewalk, about 10 m back from the gopuram, while you stand in front of the gate, so the full tower fits in a portrait frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the outer areas, but not in the inner sanctum or during ceremonies. Ask before photographing worshippers and keep a respectful distance. One reviewer found the surrounding streets didn't feel very safe at night and wouldn't go alone. Check the official site for visiting rules and dress expectations before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole tower in one shot, then count the five tiers and see how many painted figures you can spot in your close-up.
card.good_to_know: Sri Maha Mariamman is the oldest Hindu temple in Kuala Lumpur. It was founded in 1873 and moved to this site beside Chinatown in 1885. The gopuram rises 22.9 m and carries 228 idols, credited to a team led by sculptor S. T. Muniappa from Tamil Nadu. It was finished in 1972, and the temple was consecrated the next year.

card.hook: Picture a giant open umbrella and a folded one, standing side by side in a pool of still water. That's the National Mosque's star-shaped roof and minaret, and the pool will happily show you both twice.
card.stand_here: Head for the front reflecting pool at the National Mosque, right at the phone icon on the map. Face the minaret and the folded roof across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pool, minaret and roof into one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the roof tiles and minaret details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright part of the building, then slide it a little darker so the white and pale surfaces keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light. Late morning or early afternoon suits the fountains, with a nice mix of light and shadow. Whenever you go, check the official site first, because the grounds close to tourists during prayer times.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the courtyard reflecting pool with the mosque behind you, and use the front camera so the roof and minaret peek over your shoulder. The main entrance is another good backdrop for the mosque's architecture, best in early morning or late afternoon light.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the fountains facing the mosque, while you stand in front of the fountains with the whole mosque behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is fine outside the prayer hall but not inside it, and try not to photograph worshippers directly. Dress modestly (robes are provided at the entrance), and remember tourist access pauses at prayer times.
card.challenge: Get the minaret's reflection to fill the lower half of your frame, then see if a friend can guess which roof is the 'open umbrella'.
card.good_to_know: Masjid Negara was completed in 1965 as a symbol of the country's new independence. The roof is meant to recall an open umbrella and the minaret's cap a folded one. That roof was once pink, and it has been clad in green and blue tiles since the 1987 renovation. The whole place sits in about 13 acres of gardens, dotted with pools and fountains.

card.hook: Picture a long red-brick building with three copper domes, a clock tower that's trying very hard to be Big Ben, and a huge green lawn in front of it. You can't miss it, and the lawn is the secret to a great shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Dataran Merdeka (Merdeka Square) on the opposite, western side of the square, facing the building's façade. From there the building is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. Keep it in front of you as you walk so you can see the whole thing before you pick your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the far side of the square. Drop to 0.5x only if the façade won't fit. Tap 2x when you want the clock tower and domes to fill the screen.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's horizontal bands up with them, so the façade doesn't lean. Tap the brick wall, then slide it a touch darker so the sky stays blue and the domes keep their colour.

card.good_to_know: This was the government office block of British-era Kuala Lumpur, built between 1894 and 1897. The tallest of its three copper domes sits on a 41-metre clock tower designed to echo Big Ben. The front runs about 137 metres along Jalan Raja, so it's wide as well as tall.

card.hook: Look up in Kuala Lumpur and you might spot turquoise domes sitting on the skyline like giant upside-down teacups. That's the Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, and the building is a star all on its own.
card.stand_here: Stand outside the Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, within walking distance west of Kuala Lumpur railway station. Pick a spot where the whole façade and entrance fit in one frame, and face the entrance square-on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the façade and entrance. If you're close and the domes won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x for tile patterns and dome tops (higher zooms depend on your phone).

card.hook: Pink-and-white striped minarets, green trees, and glass towers peeking over the top: Jamek Mosque is the one building in Kuala Lumpur that looks good next to everything. It also sits right where two rivers meet, which is a nice bonus.
card.stand_here: Stand in Dataran Merdeka, out on the field area, and point your phone at the mosque. The clock tower and the Sultan Abdul Samad Building belong in the scene around it, so let them sneak in at the edges instead of aiming at them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the mosque and the Sultan Abdul Samad Building together. Tap 0.5x for more square and sky, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and striped minarets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the mosque on one third and the old building on the other, and keep your phone level so the minarets stand straight.
card.best_time: Night is the most recommended time, because the clock tower is lit up. Early morning and sunset are popular too, and midday is the one to skip because the sun is harsh.
card.selfie_here: Try the Masjid Jamek Lookout Point @ River of Life, on the riverside walkway where the two rivers meet. It's a walk from Masjid Jamek LRT station, and it pairs the mosque with the city skyline. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x to fit more in, and check what's behind your shoulder before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and stand on the Gombak riverbank, with the mosque's two minarets behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't go inside during prayers, so stay outside and keep to the exterior. Photos in the public areas are generally fine, but skip shots of people praying. If you go in, basic religious dress is needed, and women need to cover their heads.
card.challenge: Get both striped minarets and one shiny modern tower in the same frame, and keep the minarets perfectly upright.
card.good_to_know: Arthur Benison Hubback designed Jamek Mosque in the Indo-Saracenic style, and it opened on 23 December 1909. It was the first large mosque built in Kuala Lumpur and the city's main mosque until Masjid Negara opened in 1965. The tallest of its three domes rises to about 21.3 metres.

card.hook: Most city stations look like a shed with a clock. This one looks like a white Moorish palace that happens to have commuters hurrying through it, and honestly, the palace is winning.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, directly opposite the station's front facade on the street side, and face east. The white arches and domes should sit right in front of you, across the road from the station entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a straight, symmetrical shot of the whole front. If the full width won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the domes and arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the building up with the centre line, so all those repeating arches look perfectly matched on both sides.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon or evening. The facade faces west, so that's when it glows warmest. After dark, try night mode and brace your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Stand near the main entrance on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, beside the old cast-iron lanterns, so the ornate front is behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt up slightly so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, facing the station near the Railway Administration building, while you stand in front of the station.
card.rules_and_safety: Outside is fine for photos, but the station asks for permission to shoot inside the station area, so ask first. It's a working commuter stop, so don't block passengers or trains. The road out front is busy, so cross carefully and wait for a gap in traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get the centre line of your grid running straight down the middle of the building without any wonky edges? Bonus points if no bus photobombs you.
card.good_to_know: British architect Arthur Benison Hubback designed the station, and it was built in the 1910s as a blend of Eastern and Western ideas. Long-distance trains moved to KL Sentral in 2001, but this one still works as a KTM Komuter stop. The Railway Administration Building, the National Mosque and the Dayabumi Complex are all close by, so it fits nicely into a walk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, directly opposite the station's front facade on the street side, and face east. The white arches and domes should sit right in front of you, across the road from the station entrance.

card.hook: Here's a secret: the monument is tiny from this spot, and that's the whole charm. A 15-metre bronze peeks out over the Lake Gardens trees, and it feels much calmer than the head-on shots.
card.stand_here: Stand in Perdana Botanical Garden, on the lawns and paths across from the monument, and face back toward it. Plant yourself where the trees open up and you can see the sculpture over the green.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole garden scene. Then try 2x or 5x to pull the monument closer (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only if you want a sweeping shot of the lawn and trees.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the monument, then slide the picture a bit darker if the sky is bright, so the bronze doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. The gardens are calmer and the light is softer.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, head to the reflecting pool at Plaza Tugu Negara and stand at the pool's edge, in front of the main bronze sculpture. It's a known photo spot for symmetrical reflections. Use the front camera and check what's behind you before you snap, because the pool's position is described differently in different places.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Tugu View Cafe terrace, which overlooks the monument, to take your photo while you stand in the garden, but peek at their framing first to see if it fits the whole monument.
card.rules_and_safety: The area around the monument may be restricted or under works, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the monument on a third, and find a tree or path that leads the eye straight to it.
card.good_to_know: The National Monument (Tugu Negara) honours the people who died in Malaysia's struggle for freedom, mainly against the Japanese occupation in the Second World War and during the Malayan Emergency of 1948 to 1960. The sculpture group shows seven figures and was designed by Felix de Weldon, cast in Rome and opened on 8 February 1966. It's described as the world's tallest freestanding bronze sculpture grouping.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Perdana Botanical Garden, on the lawns and paths across from the monument, and face back toward it. Plant yourself where the trees open up and you can see the sculpture over the green.

card.hook: This building looks so official that you'd swear it was a courthouse. It was actually the government printing office, and it's still the handsomest thing on the edge of Merdeka Square.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open lawn side of Dataran Merdeka and face south. The gallery on Jalan Raja sits across the open square, with the flagpole and the historic buildings around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the building keeps its natural shape and the lawn stays in the frame. Try 2x to pick out the roofline and details. Step closer if you want the facade up close, because the square view is a wide scene.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building on your screen, then take a few shots in case people wander through your frame.
card.best_time: Go on a weekend. Traffic on the road by the nearby Sultan Abdul Samad Building is reported to be very light then.
card.selfie_here: Walk over to the red I Love KL sign at the gallery entrance and turn your back to the building. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the sign and the gallery over your shoulder.
card.challenge: Get the whole red I Love KL sign and the gallery facade in one shot, and don't let a single stranger's head sneak in.
card.good_to_know: The gallery was completed in 1898 and designed by A. C. Norman, the government architect of the Federated Malay States. It became the City Gallery in 1989. Inside, the ground floor has old photos and maps, and upstairs there's a big city model with a light and sound show. You can only enter the dark model room at the start of the show, so plan your photos around that.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open lawn side of Dataran Merdeka and face south. The gallery on Jalan Raja sits across the open square, with the flagpole and the historic buildings around it.
